name: Bartter Syndrome Type 4
aliases: Antenatal Bartter syndrome with sensorineural deafness

reference.source: Paediatric nephrology and inherited tubulopathy references
clinicalPearls: Type 4 is the Bartter subtype defined by the combination of salt-wasting tubulopathy and sensorineural deafness, because barttin is a shared subunit for chloride channels in both the kidney and the inner ear.
Presentation is typically antenatal: fetal polyuria drives maternal polyhydramnios, and affected infants are frequently born prematurely.
The biochemical signature is a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with normal or low blood pressure and markedly elevated renin and aldosterone.
The deafness is congenital and does not reverse when the electrolyte disturbance is corrected, which sets type 4 apart from types 1 to 3 that spare hearing.
Hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis tend to be less prominent than in the type 1 and type 2 forms, but type 4 carries a recognised tendency toward chronic kidney disease.
Gitelman syndrome is the key milder mimic; it involves the distal convoluted tubule and is marked by hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria rather than deafness.
Renal prostaglandin synthesis is greatly upregulated, so prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors are a therapeutic mainstay alongside salt and potassium replacement.
reference.pathophysiology: Bartter syndrome type 4 is a salt-losing tubulopathy of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Type 4a is caused by loss-of-function mutations in BSND, which encodes barttin, the obligatory beta-subunit for the ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb chloride channels that mediate basolateral chloride exit in the thick ascending limb and distal nephron and are also expressed in the stria vascularis of the cochlea. Type 4b arises from simultaneous loss of function of both ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb through digenic mutations in CLCNKA and CLCNKB. Because barttin and these chloride channels are indispensable in both kidney and cochlea, the defect produces the classic Bartter physiology, namely impaired sodium chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, a hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, secondary hyperaldosteronism and raised urinary prostaglandins, together with sensorineural deafness, the feature that defines type 4. The severe salt wasting characteristically manifests antenatally with polyhydramnios and preterm birth.
additionalDifferentials: Other Bartter subtypes: type 1 (NKCC2/SLC12A1), type 2 (ROMK/KCNJ1) and type 3 (CLCNKB)
Gitelman syndrome (SLC12A3), with hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria
Cystic fibrosis with excessive salt loss
Other renal salt-wasting states producing a pseudo-Bartter picture
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes demonstrating a hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Plasma renin and aldosterone, both characteristically elevated
Urinary electrolytes including chloride, and the urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio
Serum magnesium to help separate the condition from Gitelman syndrome
Audiometry or auditory brainstem response testing for sensorineural hearing loss
Renal ultrasound to assess for nephrocalcinosis
Genetic testing of BSND and of CLCNKA/CLCNKB
redFlags: Severe neonatal volume depletion and electrolyte derangement
Failure to thrive or frank growth failure
Undetected deafness impairing language and cognitive development
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and lifelong salt, potassium and prostaglandin-inhibitor therapy, many children achieve reasonable growth and development, but the deafness is permanent and there is a recognised risk of chronic kidney disease progressing in some patients to end-stage renal failure.
pitfalls: Attributing the deafness to prematurity or the neonatal intensive care course rather than recognising it as an integral part of the syndrome.
Confusing the disorder with Gitelman syndrome; checking magnesium and urinary calcium helps discriminate.
Failing to consider surreptitious diuretic use, which reproduces the biochemical picture.
Allowing over-correction or dehydration during intercurrent illness.
management: Sodium chloride, fluid and potassium replacement for the salt-wasting tubulopathy
Prostaglandin synthetase inhibition with indometacin to reduce polyuria and salt wasting
Potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone or amiloride to limit renal potassium losses
Audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation for the permanent sensorineural deafness
Surveillance of renal function given the recognised tendency to chronic kidney disease, with preparation for renal replacement therapy if it progresses
Multidisciplinary care including nephrology, audiology and paediatrics
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and family assessment
